To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

climate change is predicted to increase global tropospheric ozone burden and decrease global tropospheric sulfate and black carbon burdens, while the net direct radiative forcing by ozone, sulfate, nitrate and black carbon aerosols is predicted to be slightly positive, slightly negative, negative, and positive, respectively.

climate change is predicted to reduce global O 3 burdens but to increase surface O 3 concentrations in populated and biomass burning regions, and to increase the direct radiative forcing by O 3 and black carbon but to decrease the direct forcing by sulfate and organic carbon.

the global tropospheric ozone burden is predicted to decrease by 5-20%, while surface ozone concentrations are predicted to increase by 5-10%, in a CO 2 -induced climate change, with a corresponding reduction in the radiative forcing by ozone of 0.2 to 0.5 W m -2.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the effects of CO 2 -induced climate change on the global distribution and burden of tropospheric O 3 and tropospheric aerosols, as well as the radiative forcing by O 3 and the major tropospheric aerosol types, and with the implications of our predictions for global climate change.
the role of climate change in global predictions of future tropospheric O 3 and the aerosols.

the following: (1) the effects of climate on the global tropospheric ozone distribution and the resulting direct radiative forcing, (2) the effect of climate change on tropospheric aerosol burdens, (3) the effect of the climate change on the global aerosol distribution, and (4) the effect of aerosols on the radiative forcing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
climate change has significant effects on tropospheric O 3 and on tropospheric and stratospheric aerosols.
climate change is predicted to have a modest effect on the global tropospheric O 3 burden, but to have a significant effect on global tropospheric aerosol burdens.
climate change will reduce the global burden of ozone and aerosol, but increase surface layer ozone and aerosol concentrations over or near the source regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

climate change is predicted to reduce global tropospheric O 3 and sulfate burdens, while it is predicted to enhance surface layer O 1 and black carbon burdens over or near populated areas, and to increase organic carbon burdens globally.
the predicted year 2100 radiative forcing by O 3 and most of the aerosols is reduced by the climate change, while the forcing by black carbon is enhanced.
climate change has significant impacts on global O 3, aerosol, and aerosol-cloud interactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the year 21000 global direct radiative forcing by O 3 and most aerosol species are not very sensitive to the climate change, while the global mean top-of-the-atmosphere direct radiative forcing is more sensitive to changes in climate than changes in emissions.
the effects of climate on tropospheric ozone burdens are generally opposite to those on aerosols.
the year 210 global mean direct radiative forcigns are predicted to be 1-3 times larger than the year 2000 values.
